title: Open enrollment is a chance to get this ‘sneaky-good’ investment account that can be ‘better than a Roth’
description: With open enrollment season getting underway, health savings accounts are worth considering for more than just paying medical bills.That’s because you
body: With open enrollment season getting underway, health savings accounts are worth considering for more than just paying medical bills.That’s because you can invest the money in an HSA and let it grow for decades, with tax advantages that can make the account an especially powerful way to save for retirement.HSAs are "sneaky-good and very underrated" investment tools, says John Bell, a certified financial planner and founder of Free State Financial Planning. For those who are eligible, he generally puts maxing out an employer-sponsored HSA near the top of his saving priorities, just behind getting the full employer match in a 401(k), and ahead of funding a Roth IRA or taxable brokerage account.That said, you shouldn't choose a health plan just to get access to an HSA's investment potential. Whether an HSA-eligible plan makes sense depends first on your healthcare needs and the costs and coverage of the plans available to you, CFPs tell CNBC Make It.Why financial planners love HSAsLike the more common flexible spending account, or FSA, an HSA lets you set aside tax-advantaged money for qualified medical expenses, such as doctor visits, prescription drugs and dental care. One important distinction is that to contribute to an HSA, you generally must be enrolled in a high-deductible health plan. For 2027, such plans have a minimum deductible — the amount you pay out of pocket before coverage kicks in — of $1,750 for individuals and $3,500 for families. FSAs don't have the same insurance requirement and are often offered alongside more traditional copay insurance plans, which tend to come with higher premiums and lower deductibles.But HSAs differ from FSAs in a few other important ways. HSAs stay with you if you change jobs, and unlike most FSAs, they don't come with a "use it or lose it" rule requiring you to spend money in the account over a certain period. Instead, unspent money rolls over from year to year.And perhaps most importantly — and what makes HSAs "sneaky-good" as an investment tool — the money can often be invested and left to grow for years. That means an HSA can double as a long-term investment account, much like a 401(k) or brokerage account.Despite that investment potential, relatively few people take advantage of it. Just 11% of HSAs held investments as of midyear 2026, according to Devenir, an HSA research and investment firm.That’s despite some unusually generous tax advantages for investors.An HSA combines "the best parts of traditional and Roth IRAs" through what's commonly called a "triple tax advantage," says Robert Persichitte, a CFP and CPA at Delagify Financial:You don't pay federal income tax on the money you put in.Your investment gains aren't taxed. That means your money can grow and compound without Uncle Sam taking a cut along the way.The money isn't taxed when you take it out for qualified medical expenses.You don't need an employer to open an HSA, as long as you have an HSA-eligible health plan. And since 2026, people buying their own insurance have more options, as all Bronze and Catastrophic plans sold on the Affordable Care Act marketplace are HSA-eligible. But workplace HSAs can come with additional benefits: An employer may contribute money to the account, and money you put in through your paycheck can often avoid Social Security and Medicare taxes as well.If you can afford to leave money in your HSA and pay current healthcare expenses out of pocket, CFPs say there can be good reason to hold onto the money for retirement, when healthcare costs tend to rise with age.A 65-year-old retiring in 2026 can expect to spend an average of $185,500 on healthcare and medical expenses over the course of retirement, according to Fidelity Investments."Healthcare is one of the few retirement expenses we can virtually guarantee," says Corinna Rose, a CFP at Bell Investment Advisors. "Whether it's prescriptions, Medicare premiums, long-term care costs or routine medical expenses, most retirees will spend money on their health one way or another."Another advantage: There's no time limit on when you can withdraw money from an HSA to cover a past qualified medical expense. For example, if you pay a $5,000 medical bill out of pocket at age 50, you could withdraw $5,000 tax-free at age 65, as long as you kept the necessary records.Persichitte has used that strategy himself. He waited three years to reimburse himself after breaking his arm, giving the money in his HSA more time to grow.Taken together, the tax advantages are why Persichitte ranks HSAs so highly. Once you've contributed enough to a 401(k) to get the full employer match, he generally recommends maxing out an HSA before putting more money into a 401(k), Roth IRA or taxable brokerage account.How to know if an HSA is right for youAs attractive as HSAs can be as investment accounts, their investment potential alone isn't a reason to seek one out."HSAs are extremely valuable, but don't make an isolated decision on whether to own one," says Michael Schramm, a CFA charterholder and author of the forthcoming book "Emotional Finance." "Instead, step back and ask which health plan's right for you."That means comparing the actual costs and coverage of the plans available to you, including premiums, deductibles and out-of-pocket maximums, along with any money your employer contributes to an HSA, Schramm says.Higher-deductible plans generally trade lower monthly premiums for higher upfront healthcare costs, Schramm says. That can work well for someone who doesn't expect to need much medical care. But if you anticipate a lot of medical expenses, you could end up paying thousands of dollars out of pocket before your insurance starts picking up the bill.Having emergency savings matters, too. An HSA-eligible plan may be easier to manage if you have enough cash set aside to cover your deductible without taking on debt.That said, there are risks in using the money in your HSA to buy investments. Stocks and bonds have historically rewarded long-term investors, but they can lose value, and past performance doesn't guarantee future returns. Money you expect to need for near-term medical expenses may be better kept in cash.For 2027, you can put up to $4,500 into an HSA if you have self-only coverage, or $9,000 if you have family coverage. People age 55 and older can contribute an additional $1,000. Any money your employer contributes counts toward those limits.And while the money can ultimately be used for purposes other than healthcare, doing so before age 65 generally means paying income tax plus a 20% additional tax. After 65, that additional tax goes away, although nonmedical withdrawals are still generally subject to income tax.For someone who chooses an HSA-eligible plan and can comfortably handle its potential out-of-pocket costs, however, the HSA can be much more than a way to pay this year's medical bills. It can be a long-term investment account, too.

schema.headline: Open enrollment is a chance to get this ‘sneaky-good’ investment account that can be ‘better than a Roth’

title: Nvidia responds to report Jensen Huang was target of Chinese asset, says diversion allegations were 'investigated and debunked'
description: Jensen Huang, CEO of NVIDIA, presents new NVIDIA Vera Rubin DSX Pod Full-Stack Modular AI Factory as he gives a keynote address at the Berlin GPU Tech
body: Jensen Huang, CEO of NVIDIA, presents new NVIDIA Vera Rubin DSX Pod Full-Stack Modular AI Factory as he gives a keynote address at the Berlin GPU Technology Conference (GTC) on October 21, 2026 in Berlin, Germany.Sean Gallup | Getty ImagesAn Nvidia spokesperson on Thursday pushed back on a New York Times report that detailed American intelligence agencies surveilling a person close to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang because they thought she could be a Chinese intelligence asset.According to the Times report, which cited people briefed on intelligence surveillance, Alice Huang, who is linked to the Singapore-based cloud Megaspeed, developed a close relationship with Nvidia's Jensen Huang. Intelligence agencies worried that she was a spy, helping the Chinese government gain information from Nvidia and Jensen Huang, and fretted that Nvidia's CEO had access to President Donald Trump. The Nvidia spokesperson pushed back on the story in a statement to CNBC, saying that Singapore-based Megaspeed is another one of the company's regional cloud customers, and that Jensen Huang's interactions with its officials are not unusual, because he speaks with thousands of customers every year.The spokesperson added that customers don't get access to Nvidia trade secrets or relevant national security information. The report also alleged that Megaspeed was previously suspected of helping companies evade U.S. export controls on Nvidia's AI chips, which aren't allowed to be shipped to China.Nvidia said that Megaspeed had already been investigated for evading export controls. "The diversion allegations against this regional cloud were thoroughly investigated and debunked last year," the spokesperson said in a statement. Nvidia implied that the U.S. government had not briefed Nvidia on Alice Huang. "We're confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know," the spokesperson said. Nvidia has had to walk a tightrope in Washington as its AI chips have become a powerful tool for all AI developers and a bargaining chip in economic competition with China. Politicians and analysts say that Nvidia's AI chips could be used to create Chinese military AI models, or commercial AI models that could compete and eventually surpass American technology.As AI has become more important to the government, Nvidia's Huang has befriended Trump and has given pro-American speeches about building U.S. AI infrastructure. Huang has appeared with Trump at state dinners, AI summits, and international trips, all while pushing for certain Nvidia chips to get a green light to be shipped to China. Earlier this year the U.S. government cleared Nvidia's H200 chip to be shipped to China, but Chinese regulators prevented their imports. H200s are Nvidia's Hopper generation chip, not the current faster Blackwell generation currently used by American AI developers.The Nvidia spokesperson said the Chinese government is not looking for Nvidia products from regional clouds like Megaspeed. "Instead, the PRC government blocked U.S. AI chips, protecting its own industry and resulting in the largest write-offs in U.S. tech history," the Nvidia spokesperson said. Last year, Nvidia wrote off about $4.5 billion in Chinese-tuned AI chips.

schema.headline: Nvidia responds to report Jensen Huang was target of Chinese asset, says diversion allegations were 'investigated and debunked'

title: Hegseth reportedly fires U.S. top military planner as Trump downplays Iran peace talks
description: U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth gives a State of the Force address at Marine Corps Base Quantico on Sept. 30, 2026 in Quantico, Virginia.Alex W
body: U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth gives a State of the Force address at Marine Corps Base Quantico on Sept. 30, 2026 in Quantico, Virginia.Alex Wong | Getty ImagesU.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has reportedly fired the Pentagon's top military planner amid concerns that Washington may restart strikes on Iran after the midterm elections. Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia was removed as head of strategy, plans and policy on the Joint Staff, according to the Associated Press. No reason was given for his dismissal, and nobody was named as his replacement. Sylvia has now retired, ABC News reported, citing two people familiar with the matter. The AP also reported that U.S. officials have told some countries in the Middle East to be prepared for potential renewed military action against Iran after next week's midterm elections, as well as for any Iranian retaliation. Separately, the Wall Street Journal reported that Vice President JD Vance had sent a letter to Iran "engaging one of Iran's most powerful hard-liners to revive peace negotiations." Trump downplayed the idea of peace talks, telling reporters, "They need help with medical supplies and various things," adding, "he asked me what I thought. I said, 'If you want to do that, that's OK.'"On Tehran's part, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi wrote on X late Wednesday that "Iran continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed."He said that Iran remains in "close and ongoing contact with intermediaries to review ideas that can ensure implementation of our 7-Day Plan in even less than a week."The 7-day plan was proposed last month, and Tehran said the ​Strait of Hormuz could be reopened and normal maritime passage ​restored if the necessary conditions — which reportedly included ending hostilities and releasing frozen Iranian assets — are met.Tehran then would reopen the Strait to normal commercial shipping and resume negotiations with Washington.

schema.headline: Hegseth reportedly fires U.S. top military planner as Trump downplays Iran peace talks

title: Cruise companies aim to keep fuel costs down. Their strategies for doing so differ
description: Docked and arriving cruise ships in Cozumel, Mexico.Jeff Greenberg | Universal Images Group | Getty ImagesCarnival, Royal Caribbean and Norwegian Crui
body: Docked and arriving cruise ships in Cozumel, Mexico.Jeff Greenberg | Universal Images Group | Getty ImagesCarnival, Royal Caribbean and Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings posted strong earnings for their most recent quarters despite rising fuel prices. How the leading cruise companies navigate fuel costs boils down to starkly different strategies.Oil prices have skyrocketed since the U.S.-Israel war with Iran began on Feb. 28. Brent crude oil reached a six-month high on Friday, settling at $116.72 per barrel. With no clear end in sight for the conflict in the Middle East, the pressure affecting cruise ships' lifeblood seems poised to last into the holiday travel season and beyond. Both Royal Caribbean and Norwegian practice "hedging," or a strategy of using derivatives to reduce exposure to future fuel-price swings, to account for sharp price changes. Carnival CEO Josh Weinstein, on the other hand, told CNBC in an interview last month that cutting fuel consumption is the best way to avert the effects of expensive fuel."At the end of the day, fuel is an input cost for us. The best thing that we can do to control that cost is to use less," Weinstein said at the time.  Jefferies analyst David Katz told CNBC in an interview that companies that hedge do so primarily to manage the cost of fuel, but also to manage Wall Street expectations and prevent hectic stock trading based on fuel price fluctuations. "When you're public, the Street will trade your stock around based on the price of fuel," Katz said. "The Street's argument is that volatility puts pressure on your multiple." "While it is mathematically most likely true that over the long term it is more expensive," he explained. "The benefit of having less fuel volatility in the model and less trading volatility is [it's] good for your multiple."Despite the potential positives of the strategy, Carnival has maintained the stance it has held since 2019: Cutting fuel consumption works better than hedging.And Carnival's third-quarter earnings report last month suggests the strategy may be paying off. Carnival's 'maniacal' cuttingCarnival beat analysts' expectations on both the top and bottom lines for its most recent quarter and reported an all-time high net income of $1.9 billion. Weinstein told CNBC in an interview on "Squawk on the Street" following the release that the company has been "maniacal" about cutting its fuel consumption, saying it's slashed its unit fuel consumption rate by 26% since 2019. "We estimate we've saved about $700 million in 2026 based on that consumption savings rate going down since 2019," he said. Carnival spent $615 million, or about 7.3% of its revenue, on fuel in the third quarter, according to its most recent earnings release. That's an increase from the $425 million, or 6.7% of revenue, that the company spent on fuel in the fourth quarter of 2025, before fuel prices spiked. Carnival projects its fuel costs will rise to $640 million in the fourth quarter, according to its earnings release. Careful hedgingRoyal Caribbean similarly beat analyst expectations for earnings per share for its third quarter, reported Tuesday. However, it narrowly missed on revenue.CEO Jason Liberty attributed the company's beat in part to its hedging strategy during an interview on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" Tuesday morning. "We're a little bit over 60% hedged here for 2026, and so that's helping insulate us from some of the impacts on the rising fuel costs," he said. "It's obviously still impacting us," Liberty said. "[High fuel prices] evaporated a good chunk of our Q3 earnings beat into the full-year guide. But we're continuing to hedge, and we watch."Royal Caribbean spent about $347 million on fuel in the third quarter, or about 6.2% of its revenue, according to its earnings release. That compares with $293 million, or 6.8% of revenue, spent on fuel in the fourth quarter of 2025, which ended on Dec. 31.The company projects fuel costs will continue to rise to $379 million in the fourth quarter.Liberty pointed out that high fuel prices have not dampened demand from consumers for vacations."It's not that we don't see points of challenges, but really what we've seen is that even in those points of challenges, the consumer comes roaring back," he said.Royal Caribbean reported strong bookings for the third quarter and said reservations for 2027 are already up by a high-teens percentage. Norwegian's continued betNorwegian Cruise Line Holdings beat on both the top and bottom lines for its third-quarter earnings, reported on Thursday, with revenue of $2.9 billion and adjusted earnings per share of $1.12.The company has hedged approximately 48% of its fuel consumption for 2026, according to the earnings release.Norwegian spent about $196 million on fuel in the third quarter, or about 6.6% of its revenue, according to its most recent earnings release. That's a lower share of revenue than the 7.4% — totaling $167 million — spent on fuel in the fourth quarter of 2025, which ended on Dec. 31. The company projects fuel consumption to rise slightly in the fourth quarter, up to 255,000 metric tons from 239,000 metric tons consumed in the third quarter.The company is in the midst of a turnaround effort. And despite facing added challenges from the macro environment, CFO Mark Kempa said he is reassured by this quarter's results on an earnings call on Thursday. "These results reinforce our confidence in the appeal of our products and the opportunity to translate stronger revenue performance and disciplined cost management into improved profitability," Kempa said.

schema.headline: Cruise companies aim to keep fuel costs down. Their strategies for doing so differ

title: Steve Eisman gets more conservative with portfolio as AI trade nears 'tipping point'
description: watch nowSteve Eisman of "The Big Short" fame thinks the artificial intelligence trade is near a "tipping point," but he's not ready to outright bet a
body: watch nowSteve Eisman of "The Big Short" fame thinks the artificial intelligence trade is near a "tipping point," but he's not ready to outright bet against it yet."I've gotten much more conservative in my own portfolio. We have shorted against the box a whole bunch of our positions, so that our risk is much, much, much lower. But I'm not, like, net short any," he told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Thursday.Eisman's primary concern pertains to the frontier algorithm models, which are exploiting a climate of fear around their technologies, he believes, in order to set up a competitive regulatory moat against more cost-efficient products and to obscure some faltering fundamentals. Bigwigs in the tech industry have issued similar warnings.Anthropic left its latest revenue figures blank in its initial IPO filing, but Eisman believes they will show a significant deceleration from the prior quarter. Other figures in the report point to capital efficiency issue, he said.The ratio of revenue-to-equipment-expense was 2.08 in the second quarter and 1.7 in the third, marking a significant change in trajectory, Eisman said, citing an analysis he'd been given.Yet, Eisman said he was scared to make a definitive bet against the AI trade because of how intertwined it is with the market as a whole, calling it "impossible" for the technology sector to be siloed away from the broader equity market and the rest of the economy."So much of the market is on the other side, and it's still reading tea leaves. I think we're getting closer. I think the numbers from Google scared people," he said.Alphabet's stock tanked after reporting earnings on Wednesday, following a big pullback in its core advertising business as AI queries supplant internet search across its various products.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconAlphabet 5 day.Google executives said Wednesday they were running experiments to figure out what to do about it."It's worth noting the strong growth in AI mode queries had an impact because of the lower monetization we are seeing in AI mode," Philipp Schindler, Google's chief business officer, said. "Our ad experiments have shown promising results."Portions of Anthropic's recently filed S-1 struck Eisman as "extremely negative" in light of the fact that it didn't contain many metrics for the upcoming quarter that would give a clearer picture of the company's financial situation.

schema.headline: Steve Eisman gets more conservative with portfolio as AI trade nears 'tipping point'

title: ServiceNow shares plunge 25% after earnings revive AI disruption fears
description: Bill McDermott, CEO of ServiceNow speaks with CNBC on May 5, 2026.CNBCServiceNow shares sank 25% on Thursday and headed for the worst day ever after t
body: Bill McDermott, CEO of ServiceNow speaks with CNBC on May 5, 2026.CNBCServiceNow shares sank 25% on Thursday and headed for the worst day ever after the enterprise software company's third-quarter results underwhelmed, reigniting artificial intelligence disruption concerns."This was a little bit uncharacteristic for ServiceNow standards, just in terms of the lack of upside," Citi's Tyler Radke told CNBC on Thursday.Revenue grew more than 20% during the period to $4.11 billion, which was roughly in line with a $4.10 billion estimate from analysts polled by LSEG. Adjusted earnings came up short at $1.00 per share, compared to a forecast of $1.02.The results did little to overturn recent "SaaSpocalypse" fears, or concerns that new AI capabilities will upend traditional software business models.The stock drop came even after the company slightly lifted its full-year 2026 subscription revenue outlook to between $15.78 billion and $15.79 billion. Net new AI average contract value jumped 65%. One factor spooking investors is the lack of immediate payoff for the company's investments in its newly formed forward-deployed engineering team that embeds in enterprises to build AI solutions, Radke said. "It's just going to be a little bit longer of a waiting game, and so I think the market, you know, wanted to see something a little bit sooner," he said. "I think you got to wait until next year to really see that inflection."WATCH: ServiceNow shares plummet in extended trading on mixed Q3 resultswatch nowRead more CNBC tech newsAI build-out hits snag as Google and Microsoft put off raising capex forecastsAlphabet earnings miss reflects first real sign that AI is taking a bite out of searchAs Waymo expands overseas, it remains a niche cash-burning businessHands-on with Apple’s first touchscreen laptop: Touch is totally optional

title: Shell nearly doubles quarterly profit year-on-year as refining margins soar to record high
description: watch nowShell nearly doubled its quarterly profit year-on-year to $10.81 billion and saw record refining margins, the oil major said Thursday, as geo
body: watch nowShell nearly doubled its quarterly profit year-on-year to $10.81 billion and saw record refining margins, the oil major said Thursday, as geopolitical turmoil drives up crude prices and creates a fuel squeeze. Adjusted earnings, the company's measure of net profit, soared from $5.43 billion a year ago.It was the strongest profit since the second quarter of 2022, in the wake of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Analysts expected the figure to be $9.92 billion for July to September, according to an LSEG-compiled consensus.Indicative refining margins were $42 per barrel, smashing the previous record of $28.04 per barrel in the second quarter of 2022, meeting the company's forecast from earlier in the month.Shell's London-listed shares were up around 3% in morning trade, hitting an all-time high.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconShell share price.The company boosted its share buybacks, announcing a $5 billion share program to be completed over the next three months, up from $3 billion in the previous quarter.CEO Wael Sawan said the company saw strong operational performance amid "continued severe disruption to the global energy system."Other highlights from Q2:Free cash flow of $16.3 billion, up from $10 billion year-on-year.Net debt came at $39.7 billion, down from $41.75 billion in the prior quarter.Capital expenditure outlook for 2026 lowered to the $23 to 25 billion range from $24 billion to $26 billion.The reduction in net debt was impressive given Shell completed a $16.4 billion acquisition of Canadian energy firm ARC to allow it to increase production, Maurizio Carulli, equity research analyst for global energy and materials at Quilter Cheviot Investment Management, told CNBC on Thursday.Carulli said it was an impressive performance across all the company's divisions, noting he expected further "small bolt-on acquisitions" of attractive targets but not a major reshaping of its portfolio ahead. Shell recently offloaded its Indian wind and solar business and is reportedly looking to sell its UK-based chemicals joint venture with Exxon.Refined product crunch boosts industryFrance's TotalEnergies also benefited from market dynamics, more than doubling its adjusted net ​income to $9.1 billion in third-quarter results published Thursday.While its oil trading activities were steady, the oil major was boosted by "historically high refining margins in Europe and worldwide," CEO Patrick Pouyanne said.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconBrent crude.

schema.headline: Shell nearly doubles quarterly profit year-on-year as refining margins soar to record high

title: Eli Lilly hikes sales outlook, as CEO says there's room for 'dramatic' obesity market expansion
description: watch nowEli Lilly on Thursday reported third-quarter earnings and revenue that blew past estimates and hiked its full-year sales outlook, as demand f
body: watch nowEli Lilly on Thursday reported third-quarter earnings and revenue that blew past estimates and hiked its full-year sales outlook, as demand for its blockbuster weight loss drug Zepbound and diabetes treatment Mounjaro soared again. Despite that strength, sales of its new GLP-1 obesity pill Foundayo, which launched in the U.S. in April, were under Wall Street's expectations for the quarter.The pharmaceutical giant now expects 2026 revenue to come in between $91 billion and $92 billion, up from a previous guidance of $85 billion to $87 billion. Lilly projects its full-year adjusted earnings will be between $35 and $36 per share, which compares with a previous outlook of $35.50 to $36.50 per share. The company said it raised the underlying profit guidance by $4.07 per share at the midpoint, but noted that it is offset by $4.57 per share in charges tied to deals in the quarter.The company's shares rose about 7% on Thursday. Lilly's massive diabetes and obesity windfall – and market share lead over chief rival Novo – shows no signs of slowing down, even as the company grapples with lower net prices in the U.S. The pharma giant is converting its massive profits into a deal-making spree, most recently striking an agreement to buy Merida Biosciences to develop a new class of treatments for serious autoimmune and allergic diseases. Here's what Eli Lilly reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: $7.48 adjusted vs. $6.26 expectedRevenue: $24.40 billion vs. $22.61 billion expectedResilient demand for Zepbound and Mounjaro has helped fuel several strong quarters for Lilly despite lower prices for the medications in the U.S., which came after a drug pricing deal struck with the Trump administration last year. In a release, Lilly also pointed to expanded U.S. coverage for obesity care, referring to Medicare's decision to start covering GLP-1s for weight loss in July under a temporary pilot program.  "This is a program that's really working," Lilly CEO Dave Ricks said on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." "We're pleased with the early uptake and access, and I think doctors and patients are as well."Mounjaro's worldwide revenue rose 65% to $10.72 billion for the quarter, including U.S. sales of about $5 billion. That surpassed the $10.10 billion in worldwide sales and $4.79 billion in U.S. revenue that analysts were expecting for the quarter, according to StreetAccount.Mounjaro notably saw strength internationally, with sales outside the U.S. jumping 93%.Zepbound, which entered the market roughly three years ago, posted $5.35 billion in revenue for the third quarter. That's up 49% from the year-earlier period, as demand for the drug also rose while realized prices dropped. The vast majority of those sales came from the U.S. Analysts were expecting $5.09 billion in global sales for Zepbound, including $4.99 billion from the U.S., according to StreetAccount.The Eli Lilly logo appears on the company’s office in San Diego, California, Nov. 21, 2025.Mike Blake | ReutersLilly's newly launched obesity pill, Foundayo, which won U.S. approval in April, took in $184 million in sales for the third quarter. That fell under analyst forecasts of around $229 million in sales, StreetAccount estimates showed. It marks the second earnings report that includes revenue from the GLP-1 pill, which is competing head-to-head with a rival oral drug from Novo that launched in January. Total U.S. prescriptions for Foundayo and the number of new Foundayo patients in the third quarter doubled from the previous quarter, Lilly CFO Lucas Montarces said during a Thursday earnings call. Around 4 in 10 patients starting an oral obesity medicine choose Foundayo, he added.Lilly expects Foundayo to win U.S. approval for Type 2 diabetes in the fourth quarter.Lilly is working to maintain its dominance in the booming market for GLP-1 drugs, with the company holding 63% share of the U.S. obesity and diabetes drug market in the third quarter, according to an earnings presentation on Thursday. Novo's market share in the quarter was 36.6%. During the earnings call, Montarces said 7 out of 10 U.S. prescriptions for injectable obesity and diabetes drugs in the third quarter were for a Lilly medicine. Ricks told CNBC that he estimates 3% to 10% of eligible patients access obesity care in the U.S., but said the "room for expansion here of this market is dramatic." Lilly is at the front of that push, he added. Internationally, Lilly held 58.4% share of the market, while Novo had 41.6%, the presentation said. Eli Lilly's revenue in the U.S. climbed 34% to $15.1 billion. Lilly said it saw a 41% increase in volume — or the number of prescriptions or units sold — for its products, primarily for Mounjaro and Zepbound. That was partially offset by a 7% decrease in realized prices, primarily driven by Zepbound. Lilly's quarter was also boosted by a sales-based milestone payout of $410 million for its Type 2 diabetes medication Jardiance, related to the company's collaboration with Boehringer Ingelheim.Sales outside the U.S. jumped 47% to $9.3 billion, propelled by a 76% surge in volume and partly offset by a 29% drop in realized prices. The pharmaceutical giant booked net income of $6.45 billion, or $7.22 per share, for the third quarter, which includes the $4.57 per share deal charges. That compares with net income of $5.58 billion, or $6.21 per share, a year earlier. Excluding one-time items associated with the value of intangible assets and other adjustments, Eli Lilly posted earnings of $7.48 per share for the third quarter.

schema.headline: Eli Lilly hikes sales outlook, as CEO says there's room for 'dramatic' obesity market expansion

title: Alphabet falls 12%, putting it on course for its biggest ever post-earnings drop
description: watch nowAlphabet shares were down sharply following the opening bell on Thursday while Microsoft traded largely flat as investors focused on the tech
body: watch nowAlphabet shares were down sharply following the opening bell on Thursday while Microsoft traded largely flat as investors focused on the tech giants' latest spending and free cash flow numbers in their third-quarter earnings.Alphabet plummeted 12% in morning trading while Microsoft was little changed.If Alphabet closes more than 9.77% lower on Thursday, it would be its worst post-earnings reaction ever. The company went public in 2004.Microsoft reported $45.2 billion in capital expenditures and finance leases during the third quarter, which was 30% higher than a year ago, but below analyst projections of $50.67 billion. Free cash flow fell 27% to $18.63 billion but remained positive.Alphabet, in contrast, reported negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion for the third quarter, which fell much further than the $2.70 billion analysts expected by analysts. The Google parent maintained its full year capital expenditure guidance of between $195 billion and $205 billion.The earnings report comes as investors scrutinize AI spending plans of tech companies and are focusing on the returns on those investments. "Microsoft is building out its architecture in a measured way and as such contains fewer surprises," Ben Barringer, global head of technology research at Quilter Cheviot, said on Thursday. "Alphabet, by contrast, saw its share price hit after hours as a result of a fairly messy set of results and a poorly handled earnings call," Barringer added.Read more CNBC tech newsAI build-out hits snag as Google and Microsoft put off raising capex forecastsAlphabet earnings miss reflects first real sign that AI is taking a bite out of searchAs Waymo expands overseas, it remains a niche cash-burning businessHands-on with Apple’s first touchscreen laptop: Touch is totally optionalSearch under pressureAlphabet's biggest source of revenue, search advertising, grew 12% in the September quarter to $63.35 billion, but missed analyst expectations, adding further pressure to the company's shares.Philipp Schindler, Alphabet's chief business officer, said the impact on the search business was partly because of lower monetization within the company's AI Mode. He added that Alphabet is now "scaling" ads within its AI Overviews and AI Mode products, including in international markets. Google's search business has faced headwinds from the rise of other AI chatbots like OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude. People may be carrying out more search queries outside Google. Gemini, Google's own AI chatbot, has failed to keep pace."The problem for Google is it faces an innovator's dilemma and doesn't know whether to protect its core business or look to join the disruption. As such, Google has lost its edge with Gemini and is behind peers on agentic AI," Barringer said.Google's dominant market share in the search business, however, could ultimately give it a leg up over its peers, Rosenblatt Securities analyst Scott Devitt said. "I don't think it's a sea change," Devitt told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Thursday. "If it's a problem for Alphabet, it's a problem for any consumer-facing AI agent or LLM as well. And so, it's a problem that I think is ultimately going to be resolved. And when it does, Alphabet, with its 4 billion search customers that become AI customers, is in an enviable position."- CNBC's Robert Hum, Samantha Subin, Jordan Novet and Caleigh Keating contributed reporting.

schema.headline: Alphabet falls 12%, putting it on course for its biggest ever post-earnings drop

title: Amazon to report Q3 earnings after the bell with AI spend under scrutiny
description: Andy Jassy, CEO of Amazon, speaks during an unveiling event in New York, Feb. 26, 2025.Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesAmazon is slated to rep
body: Andy Jassy, CEO of Amazon, speaks during an unveiling event in New York, Feb. 26, 2025.Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesAmazon is slated to report third-quarter earnings results after the bell on Thursday. Here's what analysts are expecting, according to LSEG: Earnings per share: $1.96 adjustedRevenue: $202.31 billionWall Street is also looking at other key revenue numbers: Amazon Web Services: $45.48 billion, according to StreetAccount Advertising: $20.82 billion, according to StreetAccount Investors expect to see robust growth in Amazon's cloud segment. AWS sales are predicted to grow 38%, according to StreetAccount, compared with a 37% gain last quarter. It would mark AWS's fifth consecutive quarter of revenue acceleration. That momentum isn't expected to slow down. CEO Andy Jassy said Amazon's cloud capacity is "largely sold out" for next year, and it's received significant commitments for 2028 as well. "We always leave a certain amount for on demand and our inference service Bedrock or EC2, but largely sold out all the big chunks," Jassy said on an Andreessen Horowitz podcast last week. "A good chunk of '28 is sold out." Wall Street will be listening for any commentary from Amazon executives around AI spending. Last quarter, the company hiked its capital expenditure forecast for 2026 to $220 billion, up from $200 billion. Analysts surveyed by StreetAccount expect Amazon's capex to creep up more than $280 billion in 2027. Read more CNBC tech newsAI build-out hits snag as Google and Microsoft put off raising capex forecastsAlphabet earnings miss reflects first real sign that AI is taking a bite out of searchAs Waymo expands overseas, it remains a niche cash-burning businessHands-on with Apple’s first touchscreen laptop: Touch is totally optionalAmazon has rushed to bring more data centers online to meet surging demand for AI computing power. The aggressive spending has eaten into the company's cash flow. In July, the company reported negative free cash flow of $7.6 billion for the trailing twelve months, compared with positive free cash flow of $18.2 billion one year earlier. It's expected to be cash flow negative in the current quarter, with an outflow of $9.9 billion, according to FactSet estimates. Alphabet and Meta both reported negative free cash flow in their latest quarterly earnings reports. Microsoft said Wednesday its free cash flow declined 27% in the fiscal first quarter, but its cash flow remained positive, unlike its hyperscaler peers.   As Amazon shells out more on AI, it's steadily trimmed its headcount. The company has laid off more than 57,000 staffers since 2022, or roughly 16% of its corporate workforce. The job cuts have continued on a rolling basis this year via smaller rounds of layoffs.  The company on Wednesday laid off some staffers in its device software and services team to "operate more efficiently and better align with our product roadsmap," an Amazon spokesperson confirmed to CNBC. Fewer than 250 employees were let go as a result of the job cuts, the company said. During the third quarter, Amazon made headlines when it blocked Meta's Muse AI agent from shopping on its platform. The company said it was not given advance notice that Muse would access its webstore, and it never agreed to participate.The move is in line with Amazon's broader stance on third-party agents accessing its site. Amazon has blocked dozens of external agents, including Perplexity, which the company sued last year over allegations that the startup concealed its AI shopping bots.  Stock Chart IconStock chart iconAmazon stock chart.While it locks down its site from third-party agents, Amazon has increasingly invested in its own tools. In May, Amazon rebranded its Rufus AI shopping chatbot to Alexa for Shopping. On Thursday, Amazon said more than 400 million shoppers have used the assistant, and the number of people using Alexa for Shopping's agentic features has "grown more than eight times since the start of the year."The tool now has more than 100 shopping-related capabilities, the company said, including the ability to build gift lists, manage subscriptions and handle account changes. As rivals Meta and OpenAI push deeper into AI shopping tools, analysts have said the services could pose a risk to Amazon's digital advertising business. Users are turning to services like Muse and ChatGPT to research products, or in some cases, handing off purchases to AI agents, which means they're bypassing sponsored ads on Amazon's site. "We expect Amazon to eventually develop its own agentic shopping offering, with its proprietary purchase data and commerce infrastructure positioning it well," Deutsche Bank analysts wrote in a note last week. "The key question is whether Amazon can accommodate third-party agents on terms that preserve attractive monetization." watch now

title: The politics of President Lagarde's European Central Bank early exit  — and who could replace her
description: Christine Lagarde, president of the European Central Bank (ECB), during a rates decision news conference in Frankfurt, Germany, on Thursday, June 11,
body: Christine Lagarde, president of the European Central Bank (ECB), during a rates decision news conference in Frankfurt, Germany, on Thursday, June 11, 2026. Alex Kraus | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesEuropean Central Bank President Christine Lagarde will step down on Feb. 7 next year, she announced Thursday, formally kicking off a succession race that will be shaped by political bargaining and France's looming fiscal crisis.Lagarde has led the central bank since July 2019, steering its responses to the Covid-19 pandemic, the Russia-Ukraine war and a series of energy price shocks that sent inflation in the European Union above 11% in 2022 and spurred the end of the post-Financial Crisis era of negative interest rates.Lagarde will depart nearly nine months before her term was due to expire in October 2027, while the process to appoint her successor will begin immediately.Lagarde seeks 'freedom of expression'In a press conference Thursday following the ECB's October interest rate decision, Lagarde confirmed media reports that she was moving her departure forward because she wanted more freedom to express political opinions. Her departure will come ahead of the French presidential election next spring."The reason I'm anticipating the end of my term by leaving in February 2027 instead of October is, as I have said to colleagues, members of staff and governors, is because I want to have the freedom of speech, the freedom of expression and the freedom to engage on matters that are not monetary policy matters," she said. As ECB president, Lagarde was under the "constraint" of an "obligation of neutrality," she added."We don't get out of that mandate, because that's the price we pay for being independent. At this time, in relation to many corners of the world, not just European corners... I think that my voice can help, my actions can help in relation to principles that are dear to my heart.""One of those principles... I don't think that I can remain neutral; I don't think that I can be comfortable in that neutrality, at the present time. I'm interested in the truth, and I see the truth being very often damaged, contradicted by misrepresentation, and from the position that I have had for the last 20-plus years of my life... there are things that I can say. Whether people will listen or not is another story, but I feel that I should say those things. Voilà."Market watchers noted that the timing moves her departure before the French presidential election, in which polling suggests far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is the frontrunner. Lagarde has repeatedly downplayed any suggestion she intends to run herself. If she did run, Lagarde would face an extremely tight timeframe with the first round vote in April. An early exit means the new French president "will have no role in choosing the next ECB president — particularly significant given the political and fiscal uncertainty surrounding France," Felix Feather, Economist at Aberdeen Investments, said in emailed comments. What the ECB is looking for in a successorSenior ECB figures are already in talks about filling other senior roles, with chief economist Philip Lane and influential executive board member Isabel Schnabel, responsible for market operations, also due to step down next year. The ECB is institutionally independent, and its Governing Council comprises the six-member Executive Board and the governors of the 21 euro area national central banks. But appointments to its top jobs are made by the European Council following consultations with the European Parliament and euro area member states, with negotiations generally reflecting political bargaining over national representation and influence.Klaas Knot, president of De Nederlandsche Bank NV, on the sidelines of the Group of 20 (G-20) finance ministers and central bank governors meeting in Gandhinagar, India, on Tuesday, July 18, 2023.Bloomberg | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesSpain's Pablo Hernández de Cos and the Netherlands' Klaas Knot, who both led their respective central banks for recent stints, are widely regarded as top contenders to replace Lagarde. De Cos served from 2018 to 2024 and is now general manager of the Bank for International Settlements. Knot was Dutch central bank chief from 2011 until 2025 and is a distinguished visiting fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics.Pablo Hernandez de Cos, general manager of the Bank for International Settlements, during a farewell symposium for former De Nederlandsche Bank NV President Klaas Knot at the central bank headquarters in Amsterdam, Netherlands, on Friday, Oct. 3, 2025. Bloomberg | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesBerenberg Chief Economist Holger Schmieding said that as a result, the ECB would need to consider who was best placed to deal with potential financial turbulence."As a former chair of the G20's Financial Stability Board (FSB), Knot may have an edge in this respect," Schmieding said in a note. "The European Union is trying to guard itself at least somewhat against the risk that right-wing Marine Le Pen may win the French presidential election.""However, the ECB has no mandate and no appetite to fund French fiscal follies. In our view, the ECB would only support France if Paris returns to more sustainable policies," he added.A hawkish appointment?Knot is widely seen as the more hawkish of the pair, previously warning that the ECB risked doing too little during the inflation surge of recent years and suggesting the possibility of large rate increases.His appointment "would likely be read as hawkish and could support the euro, though a tougher stance could also add pressure to French and peripheral bond spreads," Pierre Roke, global capital markets associate at Validus Risk Management, said in a note.watch now"De Cos would signal more continuity, with a stronger focus on financial stability. With French debt under pressure and inflation still above target, rate markets would likely take more comfort in a De Cos appointment." Nationality will be another factor, ING's global head of macro, Carsten Brzeski told CNBC by email on Thursday."While Knot might find more support among Northern European governments, the question is whether De Cos will be supported by the current Spanish government.""In any case, both would bring a high level of monetary policy expertise to the table. Something that Christine Lagarde had to pick up on when already in office."Lagarde's next stepsLagarde was given a standing ovation by the Governing Council of the central bank on Thursday. "It has been a source of great pride to serve this institution. I thank all of those who have supported me on this journey over the past seven years," Lagarde said.European Council President Antonio Costa said she had provided a "steady and determined stewardship, helping to safeguard stability and the resilience of the euro area.Lagarde, born in Paris in 1956, first worked as a high-ranking lawyer before joining the French government. In 2007, she became the first female Finance Minister of a G7 country. She was appointed managing director of the International Monetary Fund in 2011, the first woman to hold the post, before joining the ECB.She faced a blow to her leadership of the central bank in 2024, when a staff survey gave a heavily critical verdict on her tenure. The survey suggested many felt she spent too much time discussing topics unrelated to monetary policy. Lagarde is viewed as a top candidate to become the next chair of the World Economic Forum, according to Financial Times reporting.

schema.headline: The politics of President Lagarde's European Central Bank early exit  — and who could replace her

title: IRS CEO Bisignano donates to Trump Accounts in his childhood Brooklyn ZIP code
description: Frank Bisignano, CEO of the Internal Revenue Service, during a House Ways and Means Subcommittee on Social Security hearing in Washington, June 10, 20
body: Frank Bisignano, CEO of the Internal Revenue Service, during a House Ways and Means Subcommittee on Social Security hearing in Washington, June 10, 2026.Tierney L. Cross | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesIRS CEO Frank Bisignano has donated to Trump Accounts for certain kids in Brooklyn, the agency announced Thursday.The Bisignano Family Fund donated $250 apiece to Trump Accounts of eligible children ages 2 to 8 living in 11234, Bisignano's hometown ZIP code, according to the release. "My life was shaped by the people, schools, and neighborhoods in Marine Park, Mill Basin, Bergen Beach, and Flatlands," Bisignano said in a statement. "This donation is an investment in the children of Brooklyn, giving them a boost in their personal wealth building journeys."Within that ZIP code, fewer than 10,000 U.S. citizens are under 10 years of age, according to CNBC's analysis of the most recent population estimate from the U.S. Census Bureau. Read more CNBC personal finance coverageIf Elon Musk gifts SpaceX stock through Trump Accounts, it will come with a catchRoth conversions aren't for everyone. When the 'juice' isn't worth it: Top advisorThe affordability crisis isn't hitting all voters equally. Here's whyMidterm elections: How affordability and the economy could affect voters' decisionsCNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 rankedCNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026The contribution will be invested in a diversified index fund, the release also said. Expanding access to Trump Accounts has been a Trump administration priority. In July, Bisignano was tasked with leading that effort. The latest Trump Account news comes weeks after the Treasury Department auto-enrolled more than 60 million children.Trump Accounts, also known as 530A accounts, are open to any U.S. citizen under 18 with a Social Security number. Children born from 2025 through 2028 may also claim a one-time $1,000 pilot program contribution from the Treasury.Families must still activate their child's Trump Account to receive contributions if eligible, according to Treasury guidance.'The tip of the iceberg'Bisignano's commitment comes on the heels of news that Elon Musk plans to give every kid in America a share of SpaceX in 2027.Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner, founder of Invest America and an architect of Trump Accounts, described Musk's gift as "the tip of the iceberg" for philanthropic gifts on CNBC's "Squawk Box" Oct. 21. Gerstner has committed about $35 million to help fund investment accounts for kids in his home state of Indiana.       More gifts are in the pipeline, Bisignano told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Oct. 8. "They range from small to mega," he said. After claiming an account, families can track deposits in the Trump Accounts app, which was designed in partnership with Robinhood."Trump Accounts is direct philanthropy, extremely efficient, direct to children...," Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev said on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Oct. 28."Excited to see Elon donation," he said. "I think there will be many others as well."watch nowThe Treasury Department in September released temporary regulations allowing Trump Accounts to hold donated individual stocks, a shift from previous guidelines that permitted only diversified, low-cost index funds. The Trump administration said the move could pave the way for more multimillion-dollar donations, with a number of philanthropists poised to participate. The latest donation comes just days before the midterm election, and Republicans fight to keep slim congressional majorities in the Senate and House.

schema.headline: IRS CEO Bisignano donates to Trump Accounts in his childhood Brooklyn ZIP code

title: Warren urges DOJ criminal probe of Bank of America over anti-money-laundering violations
description: Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., speaks at a press conference on China AI export controls at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, Sept. 23, 2026.Kevin Diets
body: Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., speaks at a press conference on China AI export controls at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, Sept. 23, 2026.Kevin Dietsch | Getty ImagesSen. Elizabeth Warren is calling on the Justice Department to open a criminal investigation into Bank of America and its executives after the banking giant admitted it willfully violated federal anti-money-laundering laws, according to a letter first shared with CNBC.The Massachusetts Democrat and ranking member of the Senate banking committee called the more than $1.2 billion in penalties imposed on the bank Oct. 13 a "slap on the wrist" and urged Attorney General Todd Blanche to determine whether criminal charges are warranted."The documented violations by Bank of America allowed illicit actors to move billions through the U.S. financial system," Warren wrote.She gave the DOJ until Nov. 12 to say whether it has already investigated the conduct and, if not, whether it plans to do so.Bank of America and the Justice Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment.The letter comes just over two weeks after Treasury regulators accused the nation's second-largest bank of years of serious compliance failures in one of the largest anti-money-laundering enforcement actions in department history.As part of its settlement with the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, Bank of America admitted it willfully violated the Bank Secrecy Act by failing to maintain an adequate anti-money-laundering program and properly report suspicious activity.Regulators said the bank failed to report in a timely manner more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions. More than $1 billion involved national-security and other high-priority risks, including activity indicative of Chinese money-laundering networks and transactions tied to the southwest border of the U.S.Treasury said Bank of America at times "prioritized its revenues" over compliance and relied heavily on law enforcement inquiries and referrals from other financial institutions to identify suspicious activity instead of its own systems.Regulators imposed more than $1.2 billion in penalties, including a record $750 million fine from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency. The actions did not include criminal charges against the bank or its executives.The bank said after the actions were announced that it had invested billions of dollars in compliance and was "far along" in addressing the problems.Warren argues the civil penalties are insufficient."Civil fines have become the cost of doing business on Wall Street," she wrote, pointing to federal law that allows criminal as well as civil penalties for willful violations of the Bank Secrecy Act.Bank of America was already operating under a 2024 cease-and-desist order over deficiencies in its anti-money-laundering controls. Regulators said this month that the bank had not made sufficient progress addressing some of those problems.

schema.headline: Warren urges DOJ criminal probe of Bank of America over anti-money-laundering violations

title: Norwegian shares surge 13% on earnings beat, guidance raise
description: Norwegian Sky, a 77,104 GT Sun-class cruise ship owned and operated by Norwegian Cruise Line, sails the Tagus River after departure from the cruise te
body: Norwegian Sky, a 77,104 GT Sun-class cruise ship owned and operated by Norwegian Cruise Line, sails the Tagus River after departure from the cruise terminal on Sept. 2, 2025, in Lisbon, Portugal.Horacio Villalobos | Corbis News | Getty ImagesShares of Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings surged about 13% Thursday after the company posted better-than-expected third-quarter earnings and raised its outlook for the full year. The cruise line reported third-quarter revenue of $2.95 billion, topping Wall Street expectations of $2.88 billion, according to analyst estimates from LSEG. Net income for the period was $491 million, or $1.07 per share.Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization was $937 million, which exceeded Norwegian's previous guidance of $874 million. Adjusted EPS was $1.12, exceeding previous guidance of 90 cents and outpacing analysts' expectations of 94 cents, per LSEG. Norwegian also raised its full-year guidance, citing its stronger-than-expected third-quarter performance. The company now expects 2026 adjusted EBITDA of $2.55 billion and adjusted EPS of about $1.70. The report said the company's bookings had "improved modestly" since its last report but remain below its optimal range. Norwegian said it will emphasize new marketing strategies, including the launch of a new marketing platform in January. It also said it anticipates that enhancements such as a new waterpark at its Great Stirrup Cay private island will support stronger demand. Also on Thursday, Norwegian announced that Chief Financial Officer Mark Kempa will step down after more than 25 years at the company. Meghan Montana, currently chief strategy officer, will take over the role starting Jan. 1.

schema.headline: Norwegian shares surge 13% on earnings beat, guidance raise

title: AI buildout hits snag as Google and Microsoft put off raising capex forecasts
description: Sundar Pichai, CEO, Google and Satya Nadella, CEO of Microsoft.Denis Balibouse | Ruben Sprich | ReutersThe past few quarters of hyperscaler earnings h
body: Sundar Pichai, CEO, Google and Satya Nadella, CEO of Microsoft.Denis Balibouse | Ruben Sprich | ReutersThe past few quarters of hyperscaler earnings have been marked by ever-increasing capital expenditure forecasts as tech giants race to build out artificial intelligence infrastructure to meet what they describe as insatiable demand.At least for the moment, Microsoft and Alphabet are telling a slightly different story. In their earnings reports Wednesday, both companies shared capex figures that came up shy of analysts' estimates. Microsoft reduced its capex forecast for the year to $170 billion from $175 billion, and Alphabet held its guidance at $195 billion to $205 billion. The numbers suggest a slowdown is nowhere in sight, but they do represent another potential point of concern for the AI buildout. Shares of neoclouds CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN all dropped after the reports, as did Oracle, which is one of the biggest spenders on AI infrastructure. Microsoft CFO Amy Hood said on the software company's earnings call that third-party providers of graphics processing units had delays that will push out some available capacity until the first half of 2027. She didn't provide names, but Microsoft relies on CoreWeave, IREN and Nebius, among others.Anat Ashkenazi, Alphabet's finance chief, told analysts that outside computing power "came online only at the very end of Q3." Alphabet shares tumbled about 10% in extended trading as the company missed on earnings and revenue and reported negative free cash flow of more than $9 billion.Plenty of Alphabet shareholders remain faithful."We are pleased with what we see and what we heard, and trust management's approach to their AI spending," Chris Ballard, managing director of Check Capital Management, wrote in an email to CNBC. Investors will get a final read on hyperscaler capex for the quarter when Amazon reports results after the close Thursday. In Meta's earnings report last week, the company said it expects full-year capex of $135 billion to $145 billion, raising the bottom of the range from $130 billion. Like with Alphabet, Meta shares sank as the company reported negative free cash flow. watch nowDelays from emerging neocloud partners have occurred before at Microsoft, but they're more critical now as Anthropic gets set to go public. Anthropic counts on infrastructure from Amazon, Google and Microsoft for much of its computing needs, alongside capacity from SpaceX, Lambda and Nscale, which filed to go public in September but hasn't updated its prospectus in weeks.At times this year, Anthropic's Claude assistant has been unavailable due to climbing demand. Rival OpenAI, which has said an initial public offering in 2027 is likely, is also in constant need of more capacity. One big challenge for the market is that the neoclouds require billions of dollars in outside capital to fuel their buildouts but don't have investment-grade credit ratings. With interest rates rising and concerns about their debt loads mounting, lenders are pulling out of the market. Last week, analysts at Gartner shared with CNBC the firm's prediction that, by 2030, 80% of neocloud companies will either be absorbed or completely cease operations. Nvidia-backed neocloud Firmus, based in Australia, withdrew plans to go public earlier this month, despite boasting large usage commitments from Meta and OpenAI.None of that is to suggest the AI buildout is over, or even close to plateauing. Microsoft's Hood said Wednesday that she sees capital spending accelerating in the first half of 2027 thanks to higher component costs and the delayed deliveries. As a group, hyperscaler capex is expected to top $1 trillion next year and, according to some estimates, continue rising from there.Despite the third-quarter capex shortfall, investors cheered Microsoft's report on Wednesday as the company beat earnings and revenue estimates, driven by 48% sales growth in its Azure cloud business."We view the quarter as further validation of Microsoft's AI-led growth opportunity," Cantor analysts led by Thomas Blakey wrote in a Wednesday note to clients. They recommend buying Microsoft stock, and they pushed up their one-year price target to $630 from $608.WATCH: Could be Google's worst earnings reaction as a public company, says Bespoke's Hickeywatch now

schema.headline: AI buildout hits snag as Google and Microsoft put off raising capex forecasts
